title: Ockham's razor

cards: The car is making a noise. A friend says it might be the transmission, or a curse, or a raccoon living in the engine. The mechanic opens the hood and finds a loose heat shield.
Start with the simplest story that explains the noise; don't add raccoons you don't need. That habit has a name, and it belongs to a friar. William of Ockham was a Franciscan, like Scotus yesterday.
His blade is called Ockham's razor.

teach.b: One of Ockham's own Latin wordings goes like this: plurality is not to be posited without necessity. In plain English, don't multiply things without need.
When two explanations cover the facts, keep the one with fewer moving parts.
The rule later got a nickname, a razor, because it shaves away whatever does no work. Ockham used it on the philosophy of his day.

Some teachers, he thought, had stacked invisible extras on top of the world, layer on layer, and he kept asking a plain question: do we need that? Often his answer was no. Yet the friar's razor didn't shave away God.

For Ockham, much of what Christians hold about God isn't proved by clever argument at all. It rests on God's free revelation, received in faith. So the razor cleared clutter out of philosophy and left trust where it was.
Jesus asked for plain speech too. Speaking about oaths in the Sermon on the Mount, he says, "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

Say yes, mean yes, and stop. And when Martha was rushing around her house with guests to feed, he told her, "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful."

teach.h: THE RAZOR LEAVES FAITH IN PLACE.
teach.b: Ockham's razor isn't a rule for faith.
It's a rule for honest thinking: explain what you need to explain, and leave the raccoons out. That closes a week that walked from John of Damascus to Anselm, Abelard and Heloise, Aquinas and Scotus.

how: Christian thinkers and teachers use the principle of not multiplying explanations in philosophy and theology, while holding that much of what they believe about God rests on revelation received in faith rather than on proof.

o: the simplest answer is always the true one
a rule that faith must be proved by argument
keep the simplest explanation that fits the facts

games.q: keep it simple — tap the pairs.
p: shaves away what does no work

s: for Ockham, the razor cut God out of the picture
he held that much about God rests on revelation received in faith, not on argument. the razor left trust where it was.
the rule is about not adding explanations without need
plurality is not to be posited without necessity.
Jesus told Martha she was troubled about many things
"Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: but one thing is needful."

games.q: you're Martha. guests are in the house, and your sister sits listening to Jesus instead of helping. you ask him to send her to the kitchen. what does he say?
o: "one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part."
"leave the guests; nobody needs to eat."
games.why: he doesn't send Mary away. "thou art careful and troubled about many things: but one thing is needful." many things, one thing.

practice: Bring to mind one story you've been telling yourself, why a friend hasn't texted back, why today feels off, and notice how many parts it has: hidden motives, secret plans, a whole plot.
Then pick up the razor and hold the simplest explanation that fits what you actually know; maybe they're busy, maybe you're tired. If you pray, you can hand the leftover worry to God.

wordCard.voice: Ockham's razor. Don't multiply things without need: keep the simplest explanation that fits, and shave off the rest.

orig.s: pluralitas non est ponenda sine necessitate
orig.say: ploo-RAH-lih-tahs non est poh-NEN-dah SEE-neh neh-kess-ih-TAH-teh
orig.note: Latin, one of Ockham's own wordings: plurality is not to be posited without necessity.

carryVoice: Your line: keep it simple. One thing is needful. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.
